# Still

There's a word I keep turning over: *still*. Four meanings live inside it, and they shouldn't get along, and yet they do.

The first is stillness proper. Motionlessness. *Hold still.* We say it to children we're trying to photograph, to a dog with a burr in its ear, to our own hands when the coffee cup is too full. Still water, which is the water that shows you your face. There's something faintly threatening in the word used this way — to be told to hold still is almost always to be told that something is about to be done to you. The doctor's needle, the barber's razor, the parent's washcloth. Stillness is the posture of submitting to another person's careful hands.

The second meaning is continuation. *Are you still here?* This one has an ache in it that the first one doesn't. It always implies a clock somewhere in the background, ticking, and a mild surprise that the clock hasn't yet been obeyed. *She's still asleep. He's still in love with her. The store is still open.* Every use of *still* in this sense carries a little ghost of its opposite — of the not-still, the no-longer, the world in which the store closed at six like it was supposed to. When you say a thing is still happening, you're admitting you'd half expected it to stop.

The third is *nevertheless*. The pivot word, the word of stubbornness. *It rained the whole week. Still, we went.* This is the *still* of the reluctant conjunction, the sentence turning on its heel. It's a small word doing enormous work: everything before it gets acknowledged and then, without being denied, gets overruled. I love this *still*. It's the most human of the four, because it's the sound of a person holding two incompatible things at once and refusing to drop either. *I know. Still.* You can end a sentence there and be perfectly understood.

The fourth is a machine. A copper vessel with a long neck, in which a liquid is heated so that some part of it leaves and comes back purer. A still. This one seems like it must be related to the others — the patient apparatus, the waiting, the drip that requires you not to hurry. It feels like it belongs to the family.

It doesn't. That's the thing I find beautiful.

The first three are genuine relatives. They all come from an old Germanic word for fixedness, for standing, cousin to *stall*. Motionlessness came first; then "without interruption," which is motionlessness stretched out along a time axis instead of a spatial one; then, later, that lovely swerve into "nevertheless," where persistence becomes argument. You can watch the word walk from the body to the calendar to the mind. That's a real lineage.

But the still in the distillery came in from Latin, by a different door entirely. *Distillare*: to drip down. From *stilla*, a drop. Nothing to do with stillness at all. English shortened *distill* to *still* and the two words happened to arrive at the same three-letter address, like strangers with identical names who are forever getting each other's mail.

I find this more moving than if it had been a true relation. Because the resonance is real even though the relationship isn't. It *is* apt that the machine of patient purification shares a name with motionlessness and persistence and nevertheless. The aptness just wasn't planned. Nobody built it. Two unrelated histories collided in the middle of a language and produced a coincidence so fitting that for a few hundred years everyone has been quietly enjoying it without noticing.

This happens more than we admit. A great deal of what feels like meaning is accident that has been standing in the right light. We're pattern-hungry animals, and the world is dense enough that patterns show up whether or not anyone put them there. The usual response to this observation is deflationary — *ah, so it's meaningless* — but I don't think that follows. The coincidence between the still and stillness didn't need to be authored to be true. The two meanings really do illuminate each other. Distillation really is a discipline of not-hurrying. The rhyme is unearned and it still works. *Still* it works.

And then there's *still life*, which comes from the Dutch *stilleven*, and which the French, characteristically, call *nature morte* — dead nature. Two ways of naming the same painting: a bowl of lemons and a dead pheasant and a glass half full of wine. The Dutch saw quietness. The French saw a corpse. Both were looking at the same lemons. I think about this whenever I catch myself believing that my description of something is the thing itself.

A photograph is a still. Cinema borrowed the word for the single frame lifted out of the moving reel — the moment made unable to continue. Which brings the whole thing back around, because there is the *still* of persistence and the *still* of arrest, and a photograph is somehow both: the instant frozen precisely so that it can go on existing. To stop something is sometimes the only way to keep it. The word contains its own paradox and doesn't seem embarrassed about it.

I don't have a thesis. I've been circling one word for a thousand-odd words because I like how much fits inside it, and because I suspect this is what most thinking actually is — not the construction of arguments but the slow rotation of an object in the light, waiting to see which facet catches.

But here's the thing I keep coming back to. All four meanings converge on a single instruction, which is: *don't move yet*. Hold your position. Let the vapor rise and cool on its own schedule. Keep being what you were despite the hour. Grant the objection and refuse it anyway.

Nearly everything I find worth admiring in people has this shape. Not force, not speed — duration. The willingness to remain. Grief that doesn't resolve on schedule and isn't rushed. Attention held past the point of comfort. The friend who is *still* there, at two in the morning, on the phone, having heard the story before.

It rained the whole week.

Still.
